deep.reconstruction:
This page holds raw observational and reduction scratch work in practical astronomy. It is not pure mathematics. It continues the previous page, which clears a lunar distance: there are altitudes a, b, the horizontal parallax 56'40", a distance D = 77°8'47", and half-sum quantities S = (A+B+D)/2 in Borda's style. That page ends with 'Pariser Zeit 2h52'31"' against local true time 3h23'0", a difference of 30'31" in time. That is essentially the longitude of Göttingen east of Paris, about 30m. So this page belongs to a determination of longitude by lunar distances with a reflecting instrument (sextant or circle), probably with an artificial horizon. The blocks are as follows.

(A) Upper left, under a heading involving the sign ♌ (possibly 'Cor Leonis' = Regulus; the heading is uncertain). The first row, 84°50', is struck out. Then come readings h = 85°10', 85°20', …, 86°10' in 10' steps against clock readings (minutes and seconds) 17'31", 18'11", 18'50", 19'29", 20'8½", 20'49", 21'29½". The successive time differences are 40, 39, 39, 39½, 40½, 40½ seconds. So the readings rise at a steady ~15' per minute. That is too fast for a single altitude at Göttingen's latitude, so these are most likely double altitudes in an artificial horizon, about 7.5'/min in true altitude. The equal steps of the instrument reading are typical of altitude series for clock correction (time determination). The mean of the 7 pairs (my addition) is reading 85°40' at about 19'29.7".

(B) Below that: 34'55" and 28'35" give 31'45" and 3'10". Check: (34'55" + 28'35")/2 = 31'45" and (34'55" − 28'35")/2 = 3'10". This is the standard index-error determination from the Sun's diameter measured 'on' and 'off' the arc. The index error is half the difference, 3'10". Half the sum, 31'45", is the Sun's apparent diameter, giving a semidiameter of 15'52.5" (my inference), which is plausible.

(C) Centre top, headed by a word read as 'brevy' (uncertain). Times 46m34s, 48m3½s, 49m3s, 51m9s pair with readings 60°49'40", 60°40'0", 60°30', 60°20'. The readings fall by about 30' in about 4.6 min. This is again consistent with (double) altitudes, here of a body past the meridian, for time.

(D) Top: 5.10.36 with 58'42" and the further seconds-readings 48, 39, 36, 29 (minutes understood). These look like a short series of repeated readings to be meaned.

(E) Times 5h49m0s, 6h4m50s, 6h5m24s, 6h6m1s. The last three are spaced 34s and 37s apart. They are probably associated with readings that were not written or are lost.

(F) Main central series of lunar distances:
- 5h46m53.6s, 88°49'0"
- 6h7m45s, 88°57'38"
- 6h9m37s, 88°58'15"
- 6h11m29s, 88°59'18"
- 6h16m28s, 89°1'3"
- 6h34m19s, 89°8'25"

From the first to the last the distance grows by 19'25" in 47m25.4s, about 0.41'/min or 24.6'/h. That is the expected rate of change of a Moon–Sun or Moon–star distance, so this is a series of observed lunar distances. The individual rates (0.41, 0.33, 0.56, 0.35, 0.41'/min) show ordinary observational scatter. The jottings 0.8 and 18 below are presumably small corrections.

(G) 24'36" and 4'12" with 618, 103, 25. These are a small subtraction or proportional-part computation; I cannot reconstruct it with certainty.

(H) Right: 79°31'25" marked ♌ (perhaps a distance to Regulus), followed by 75°10', 75°30' (third digit uncertain), 74°50'.

(I) Under a moon sign: times 54'44", 56'41", 59'35", 1'32" (next hour) against readings 70°40', 71°10', 71°40', 72°10'. These are steps of 30' in about 2–3 min, i.e. rising (double) altitudes of the Moon, needed for clearing the lunar distance. The time differences are 1m57s, 2m54s, 1m57s, so the readings are unevenly spaced in time; this suggests a slip or a missed contact at the third reading.

(J) Top right: 11650, 2846, 4384, 265… and the fractions 2/5 + 1/43 = 91/215 ≈ 0.42326 and (lower left) 2/5 + 1/46 = 97/230 ≈ 0.42174. These are apparently interpolation factors (proportional parts of a time interval) written as a sum of unit-like fractions. One is queried with '?', so Gauss was checking which value applied. Their exact source cannot be determined from the page.

In short, the page records the field data of a time-and-longitude determination: altitude series for time, index error, a series of lunar distances, and Moon altitudes, to be reduced as on the preceding page.
errors: No outright arithmetic errors detected in the verifiable pieces; the index-error half-sum and half-difference (31'45", 3'10") are exact.
In block (I) the time intervals between equal 30' steps are 1m57s, 2m54s, 1m57s. The middle interval is anomalous, suggesting a misread or slipped observation (or a transcription issue in '59 35').

In the lunar distance series the 6h11m29s reading (rate 0.56'/min against neighbours of ~0.35–0.41'/min) looks like a slightly discordant observation, which is normal scatter rather than an error of computation.
First row 84°50' in block (A) is struck out by Gauss himself.

results.what: Index error and solar diameter from on-arc/off-arc readings of the Sun's diameter: IE = (on − off)/2, diameter = (on + off)/2
results.modern_name: Sextant index error determination by the Sun's diameter
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th-century nautical/geodetic practice (Hadley-sextant users; e.g. Maskelyne's instructions)

results.what: Series of (double) altitudes at equal instrument steps with clock times, for clock correction and time determination
results.modern_name: Time determination by single/equal altitudes with artificial horizon

results.what: Series of observed lunar distances changing ~25'/h, with Moon altitudes, feeding the longitude reduction of the previous page (Paris vs local time, difference ≈30m31s)
results.usually_credited_to: Tobias Mayer / Nevil Maskelyne (1760s); reduction formulas Borda, Dunthorne

deep.surprise_reason: Routine observational and reduction scratch work (time determination, index error, lunar distances for longitude). Gauss's practical astronomical and geodetic observing at Göttingen is well documented, and nothing here is mathematically novel.
